sections.h2: Where a deed gets recorded in Trumbull County
sections.html:
Deeds for land anywhere in Trumbull County are recorded at the Recorder's Office, 160 High Street NW, Warren, Ohio 44481. Doors are open weekdays, 8:30 a.m. through 4:30 p.m. New filings stop at 4:00 p.m. while the staff close out the day.

The office records, files and indexes papers that touch real estate, including deeds, mortgages, easements, leases, powers of attorney, plats and mechanic's liens. The index follows owner names rather than street addresses, so searching one person lists every parcel held. Images and data are online for every record except military discharges, reaching back to 1795, the year of the first recordings in the county.

A seller does not usually deal with the recorder directly. Usually the title company walks the deed through the tax map office and auditor, then files it here. Knowing the sequence helps when a closing date is tight.

sections.h2: What does the Recorder charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
Fees went up April 1, 2025: the recorder now takes $39 for the opening two pages of most documents and $8 for each later page. Senate Bill 94 supplied the extra $5, a preservation surcharge layered over the base fees in Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Sample totals:

Trumbull County Recorder fees
Document or serviceFee
1 or 2 pages$39
3 pages$47
5 pages$63
10 pages$103
Marginal reference on a separate instrument$4 each
Document that misses layout standards$20 extra

Other charges:

  • Certified copy: $2 a page, plus $1 for the seal.
  • Copies made with staff help: $2 a page.
  • Plat recording: $0.10 per square inch, minimum $40.
  • Military records: no fee.
  • Cards: a 2.60 percent convenience fee applies to debit and credit payments.

Cash, checks, money orders and e-checks are also accepted. By mail, an underpayment or overpayment sends the package back unrecorded, and the office will not mail cash back, so send a check or money order.

Any document that falls short of the state formatting standard is recorded with a $20 surcharge, and the same charge applies automatically to e-filed documents that miss the mark. The recorder posts the checklist on its requirements page.

  • Ten-point type or bigger, on letter or legal paper.
  • Blue or black ink, no highlighter.
  • Three blank inches at the head of page one, which county staff use for their stamps.
  • An inch and a half of space across the top of later pages, and one inch along the edges.
  • Notary seals that print cleanly and do not overlap the embossed seal.
  • A readable printed name beneath any hard-to-read signature, and a line near the end naming who prepared the instrument.

The checklist skips plats, discharge papers, government-issued records, anything from a court or taxing authority, and papers signed before mid-2009.

sections.h2: How a deed moves through the county offices
sections.html:
A deed cannot go straight to the recorder. It must carry the required forms and a legible copy of the last deed of record, and it goes first to the Tax Map Office, then to the Auditor, and last to the Recorder. The auditor's conveyance room is upstairs in the Administration Building, phone 330-675-2420. Questions about legal descriptions go to the tax map department at 330-675-2473.

  • The Tax Map Office reviews the legal description and parcel split, if any.
  • The Auditor collects the conveyance fee and stamps the deed. The price is $4.00 for every thousand dollars of value conveyed plus $0.50 per parcel, and an exempt conveyance pays just the parcel charge.
  • The Recorder files and indexes the deed after that.

Two checks are needed: one to the Auditor for conveyance fees, a second to the Recorder for recording. Mailed transfers are accepted at the 160 High Street NW address with a stamped return envelope. Counties may add a transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100 of value under section 322.02. Ask the staff in the conveyance room whether Trumbull County charges one on your deed.

The recorder tries to send originals back within 24 business hours, and most filings go out the same day. Deeds that must pass through other offices first can take longer. The office also takes eRecording through four partner vendors and accepts most documents, transfer documents included.

sections.h2: What the Recorder will not do for a seller
sections.html:
Recorder staff may not run title searches under state law, so nobody there can certify that a parcel is clear. Employees also cannot draft or notarize a deed, choose a form or advise on one, and the office sells no blank forms. Attorneys and title companies handle those jobs.

A few points to know before listing a house:

  • A deed is binding even when unrecorded, but recording protects the new owner, because the public record would otherwise still show the former owner holding title and able to borrow against it.
  • A recorded deed cannot be edited. To add or remove a name, record a fresh deed. Errors in a recorded deed are a matter for an attorney.
  • A deed covers the land, so building a house later does not produce a new deed.
  • Re-recording is allowed only when the document itself states the reason, and costs the standard fee plus $4.

Torrens (registered land) filings were taken through June 1996 and are no longer accepted.

A mortgage is released when the lender records a satisfaction. The lender must start it. Some lenders mail the release to the borrower, who can carry the original to the recorder along with the fee and a stamped return envelope. After a payoff, ask the lender how the release will be filed, then check with the recorder that it landed.

Only the party that filed a lien can remove it, and the recorder does not report liens to credit bureaus or notify them when one is released. Mechanic's liens can be checked in the recorder's search, but judgment and other liens may sit with the Clerk of Courts or at the state level, which is why a title examiner is worth hiring. Deed restrictions and oil and gas interests also need an examiner's review.

Warren is both seat and largest city of Trumbull County, which fills a square block of Ohio's far northeast corner. Cities include Cortland, Girard, Hubbard, Niles and Warren, with villages such as Lordstown and Newton Falls. The county has 198,972 residents, and owners hold 71.3 percent of occupied homes. The typical owned home is valued at $141,800 and median rent is $797 a month.

Before you list, gather your last recorded deed and any lien releases, which saves a second trip through the county offices. If the house needs work and you plan a quick cash sale, the same sequence applies: tax map office, Auditor, then Recorder.

faqs.q: What is the Trumbull County fee for filing a deed?
faqs.a: A deed of one or two pages is $39 at the Warren office, and every page beyond that adds $8. A reference to an earlier recorded paper adds $4, and a deed that ignores the layout checklist picks up a $20 surcharge. The auditor's conveyance fee is a separate check.

faqs.q: Does Trumbull County record deeds by mail?
faqs.a: Yes, mailing works. The package needs a deed already cleared by the tax map office and the Auditor, a check for the precise sum, and a return envelope with postage. Wrong amounts come back unrecorded.

faqs.q: Can the Trumbull County Recorder do a title search for me?
faqs.a: No. State law prohibits the office from doing real estate title searches. Title companies and attorneys search the records and back the result with title insurance. You can search the county's online index yourself.

faqs.q: How long does Trumbull County take to return a recorded deed?
faqs.a: Most documents go out the same day. The recorder aims to return originals within 24 business hours, and deeds that must clear other offices first may take a little longer. Originals go back to whoever submitted them.

faqs.q: Is a deed valid if I never record it in Trumbull County?
faqs.a: A deed binds the parties even when unrecorded, but recording is advised. Until it is on record, the public index still shows the former owner, who could take out a mortgage or have a judgment attach to the property.
